newsitem.title: UK: UK budget largely benevolent for investment firms.
newsitem.headline: UK budget largely benevolent for investment firms.

text.p: Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's UK budget for the coming year was seen as largely neutral and possibly benevolent for the retail investment management industry, trade bodies and fund managers said.
"We were not looking for any major changes," said Fiona Munro at the Association of Investment trust Companies (AITC).
"It was broadly a good news budget in that it gave people more disposable income but there was little additional incentive for them to save it."

Clarke cut the standard rate of income tax by one pence in the pound, raised the personal allowance on income on which no tax is paid, lifted the tax thresholds for lower and upper rate taxpayers and for inheritance tax.
Retail financial service providers had hoped for a reduction of capital gains tax (CGT), which was left unchanged.

"That is positive, in that the tax relief is the main attraction of PEPs (personal equity plans)," said a fund manager. "But we had hoped for a small reduction in CGT and the PEP threshhold hasn't been raised."

Several investment houses said they would wait to see the detailed text of the Budget. "We were expecting a change in capital gains tax and we are not ruling it out until we have seen the full text," said a spokeswoman at Invesco.
The giant M&G personal finance group concured.

Simon Haslam, chief financial officer at Fidelity Investments, said the Red Book showed a slight extension of the window to convert unit trusts to Open Ended Investment Companies (OEICs), which are due to be launched on January 7.
"That has widened to 2-1/2 years from two years, which is welcome, but no big deal," Haslam said.
There is a small change in the way the stamp duty works for unit trusts buying their units back from investors and then cancelling the units.

"It will be simplified and result in a non-recoverable tax but at a lower rate, Haslam said. "If it goes through exactly as envisaged it might penalise cash unit trusts and bond unit trust and effectively increase the spread the manager will have to put into his pricing. But we are talking about 25-30 basis points."
He said that on pension fund contributions "they have increased earnings cap broadly in line with inflation and I think there is a long term problem building there."
"Earnings are going up faster than the cost of living and more and more people over time are going to bump up against that limit on how much they can put in their pension scheme."
John Spooner, director of Quester Venture Capital Trust said he believed the Budget press releases contained a small change for venture capital trusts (VCTs).
"It appears that if an existing VCT raises more money it will be able to take another three years to invest it," he said.
"So you have three years to invest your initial capital and another three years to invest the second tranche. It all helps to give the investor more time to make sound decisions."
The British Venture Capital Asoociation had been pushing for just such a concession, he added.

For institutional investors, the budget was likely to be seen as "very cautious, very prudent", said Jeremy Batstone at NatWest Stockbrokers. "Clarke has resisted the pressure and the worst excesses of his backbenchers."
He said that with the help for small businesses, fund managers might look again at the UK small cap sector.

Despite increased taxes on insurance premiums, if the government could "bite the bullet on inlfation" with possible interest rate rises, funds might take on more exposure to insurance compnaies and retail banks.
"The demutualisation of building societies over the next year means institutions may not want to be underweight that sector," Batstone added.
